newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany to meet deficit despite revenue blow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany to meet deficit despite revenue blow.

text.p: Germany vowed on Friday to keep its budget deficit on target next year for European monetary union, despite new numbers which showed tax revenues will undershoot earlier projections by over 10 billion marks ($6.6 billion).

Finance Minister Theo Waigel pledged to hold the federal deficit to his target of 56.5 billion marks and appealed to Germany's states and local government to do their bit to keep total borrowing below Maastricht treaty limits.

"The federal government will, despite lower tax revenues, hold firm to the essential goal of reducing the deficit. States and local governments must equally meet their responsibility to save," he said after the latest tax revenue estimate.
"We must jointly ensure that the preconditions on the way to investment, jobs and European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) are established," he added in a statement.

An independent working panel said that total tax revenues in 1997 would be 822 billion marks, over 10 billion marks shy of its forecast last May. Revenues this year are likely to be five billion marks lower than expected at 805 billion marks.

Waigel said that the 1997 revisions had already been covered by the government's Programme for More Jobs and Growth -- a bundle of job-creation and savings measures drafted last spring which has mostly been passed into law.
Further savings of seven billion marks have been included in the 1997 draft budget, but Waigel said he was still seeking cuts of three billion marks in spending next year.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl chaired a cabinet meeting on Friday morning which reached broad agreement on the cuts, but a final decision is only expected on Sunday after review by the leaders of the three parties in his centre-right coalition.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe got off with cuts of only about 200 million marks, but said he would still have great difficulty finding funds to buy new equipment and keep German peace-keeping troops in Bosnia. "We have to save everywhere -- there's no way around it," he said.
A finished budget draft will be put to parliament's budget committee next week, and a final reading of the measure will be held in late November.
Although the coalition has set aside internal feuding over tax plans, Waigel is still under immense pressure to produce credible policies after he missed borrowing targets this year.

He has based his demand for a tough stability pact to discipline EMU members on the assumption that Germany will meet Maastricht's deficit limit of three percent of gross domestic product. This year's deficit will be about four percent.
He later reiterated Germany wanted to hold its total public deficit -- the borrowing by federal, state and local bodies -- down to 2.5 percent of GDP.
But even the future European central bank, the European Monetary Institute, said this week Germany required "strong and sustained action" to turn around fiscal trends.
Unemployment, which has climbed to post-unification highs, is pressuring the state's revenue base, and analysts noted tax inflows were failing to respond to emerging economic recovery.

They said the revenue forecast was down, even though it was based on growth expectations which are more optimistic than six months ago. The panel expects growth of between one and 1.5 percent this year and 2.5 percent in 1997.
"I would presume that there were some miscalculations (in the previous estimate). This is certainly not coming from the economy," Rolf Schneider of Dresdner International Investors.

Ernst Schwanhold, economics spokesman of the opposition Social Democrats, accused Waigel of making over-optimistic assumptions already put out of date by weak industrial and jobless figures this week.
With the 14-year Kohl alliance under siege over its financial competence, commentators are calling for urgent action on passing a major tax reform it now plans in 1999.

"The coalition has one last chance to win back its reputation: It must start its tax policy all over again and design an income tax reform that really deserves the name," the Handelsblatt daily commented. ($1=1.5104 Mark)
